claims.text: The target Mg-containing lightweight HEA has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The as-cast alloy is a non-equilibrium, primarily homogeneous solid solution containing only minor heterogeneities or minimal intermetallic phases.
Thermal exposure at 600–800°C for 10–12 hours activates elemental diffusion without remelting the alloy.
Thermally activated diffusion causes Mg and other elements to segregate from the metastable solid solution.
Diffusion-induced segregation produces stable intermetallic compounds at the expense of the initially homogeneous solid solution.
The thermally formed intermetallic compounds are enriched in Mg and potentially Gd or other constituent elements.
The intermetallic compounds preferentially emerge at grain boundaries and other interfaces during thermal aging.
Mg-enriched intermetallic regions promote nucleation of Mg-rich oxide phases during high-temperature oxidation.
Oxidation of the aged microstructure produces a more continuous and protective Mg-rich oxide layer than oxidation of the as-cast microstructure.
The more continuous Mg-rich oxide layer improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast alloy.
Chemical and electrochemical differences between the intermetallic regions and the matrix establish localized micro-galvanic cells in aqueous chloride solution.
Micro-galvanic coupling accelerates localized corrosion at intermetallic/matrix interfaces.
Thermal aging reduces corrosion resistance in room-temperature 3.5 wt% NaCl relative to the as-cast baseline.
Reduced corrosion resistance would be manifested by higher corrosion current density or lower electrochemical impedance.
